rawContent: Journalists reporting on #metoo: please, for the love of all that's decent, get trauma informed.

Journalists reporting about #metoo need to understand that it's terrifying to disclose. Being retaliated against is only one terror, and there are more. Being disbelieved, dismissed, having the harm minimized: ending up isolated. That is terrifying on a somatic level.

Journalists reporting on #MeToo need to understand the internal conflict survivors experience between the terror that the person who harmed them is still out there, could still harm them or others, and the terror that they could be abandoned by their community for speaking up.

Many journalists who cover #MeToo have been rightly challenged on methods -- for pressuring survivors, especially telling them that it's up to them to stop the harm they had to survive so that it doesn't happen to others. This needs to stop.
Journalists covering #MeToo have helped scale the whisper network but the heroes are survivors.

How many journalists covering #MeToo lay out how journalism works so survivors can make an informed decision about whether to share their story? Do they say "At some point, the publication will have invested so much in this that we may run the story even if you change your mind"?

Many journalists who cover #MeToo frame reporting as "justice" for survivors, not mentioning to them until much later that many mainstream outlets require a journalist to reach out to the person who did the harm for comment.

Journalists covering #metoo profit (rarely financially, but certainly in name recognition) and survivors, more often than not, discover that having their story told removes their agency on a very real level.

For example, survivors are not asked by journalists covering #metoo when it's the best time for the story about the harm they experienced to run. Most survivors don't even get a courtesy heads up from a journalist that the story is going out the next day. The story just runs.
But stories take time and trauma presents a complicated landscape. Journalists reporting on #MeToo need to understand this so that they don't compound the trauma in the process of reporting.

Another reason survivors sometimes approach journalists who cover #MeToo is that being harmed is disempowering and doing something about it -- especially with someone who has helped others in a similar situation -- can return a sense of agency to a survivor.

What survivors tend to look for when they are considering whether to disclose is connection. They want to talk to someone who will believe. A journalist who covers #MeToo can appear like someone who is trustworthy and safe to disclose to.

If you are a journalist covering #MeToo you should listen attentively to survivors who choose to speak up about their experiences with you and other journalists. You should ttake in their words and think deeply on them. This is how you grow.
This is another example of something that affects survivors deeply that journalists covering #MeToo need to recognize: https://t.co/gOR1t1395k

@docfreeride The fact that a journalist writing on #MeToo  views the critique that he fails to center survivors as a "trope" and a "meme" is bizarre given this question is fundamental to this work? I'm so angry and filled with sorrow about this.
